title: Margin, PDT, settlement, cash
teaches: Know the account rules before they bite: what margin lends and when it calls, how FINRA replaced the pattern day trader rule in 2026, how T+1 settlement trips up a cash account, and why going to cash is a trade with a cost.

facts.quote: new intraday margin standards to replace in their entirety the outdated day trading margin requirements, including the day trade count requirements for designating a customer as a “pattern day trader” and the $25,000 pattern day trader minimum equity requirement
facts.claim: FINRA's new intraday margin standards replace the old day trading rules entirely, the pattern day trader trade count and the $25,000 minimum included.

facts.quote: Effective Date: June 4, 2026; Phase-in Period: Ends October 20, 2027
facts.claim: The new rule took effect June 4, 2026, and brokers may phase it in until October 20, 2027.

facts.quote: Members that need more time to implement the rule change will be permitted to phase in their implementation over a period of 18 months, until October 20, 2027.
facts.claim: Brokers that need more time can take up to 18 months to switch.

facts.quote: The new rule does not change the regular maintenance margin requirements as they exist today, but rather supplements them.
facts.claim: The regular maintenance margin rules stay the same; the intraday rule adds to them.

facts.quote: There’s no $25,000 minimum equity requirement for day trading.
facts.claim: Under the new rule there is no $25,000 minimum to day trade.

facts.quote: There’s no "pattern day trader" designation based on counting trades. Instead, your firm monitors your account to ensure you maintain adequate equity during the trading day relative to your actual positions.
facts.claim: The new rule drops the trade count and checks your equity against your positions during the day.

facts.quote: If an imbalance occurs and your account doesn’t have enough equity to cover your open positions, you have an "intraday margin deficit" that you're expected to satisfy as promptly as possible.
facts.claim: Too little equity for your open positions during the day is an intraday margin deficit, and you must cover it promptly.

facts.quote: If you repeatedly fail to satisfy intraday margin deficits promptly, this may result in your account being restricted for up to 90 days.
facts.claim: Repeatedly missing intraday margin deficits can get the account restricted for up to 90 days.

facts.quote: Your firm might continue operating under the old day trading margin requirements during the transition, or they might choose to migrate to the new system sooner.
facts.claim: During the transition, your broker may still run the old day trading rules.

facts.quote: However, $2,000 is the minimum equity required to engage in leveraged trading (trading on margin).
facts.claim: You need at least $2,000 of equity to borrow on margin.

facts.quote: You can trade in a margin account with less than $2,000 in equity, but you cannot use leverage—you must trade only with the cash you have available
facts.claim: Under $2,000 of equity you can still trade in a margin account, but only with your own cash.

facts.quote: you must hold adequate maintenance margin—a minimum equity level of 25 percent of the current market value of the long margin-eligible equity securities in your margin account—throughout the entire trading day, not just at end of the day.
facts.claim: Under the new rule, the 25% maintenance level applies all through the trading day, not just at the close.

facts.quote: Your firm has the authority to impose higher requirements if they choose.
facts.claim: Your broker can set higher requirements than FINRA's.

facts.quote: When you buy securities in a cash account, you must pay for securities in full before selling them.
facts.claim: In a cash account, you pay in full before you sell.

facts.quote: You can also incur what’s known as a “good faith violation” if you purchase a security with cash from a transaction that hasn’t settled yet and then sell the security before the proceeds used to fund the purchase have settled.
facts.claim: Buying with unsettled cash and selling before that cash settles is a good faith violation.

facts.quote: The current settlement time for most equity trades is T+1, or the next business day.
facts.claim: Most stock trades settle T+1, the next business day.

facts.quote: if you want to engage in intraday trading in a cash account, be sure that you fully pay for those securities at the time of purchase with settled funds.
facts.claim: To day trade in a cash account, pay for each buy with settled cash.

facts.quote: To trade using margin (funds borrowed from your firm), you must maintain a minimum of $2,000 in equity in your margin account.
facts.claim: Trading on margin needs at least $2,000 of equity in the account.

facts.quote: Your brokerage firm may require higher minimum equity amounts—often called "house" requirements—depending on the firm's policies and your account activity.
facts.claim: Brokers can require more equity than FINRA's minimum; these are house requirements.

facts.quote: However, margin trading comes with its own set of risks, including the potential to lose more than your original investment.
facts.claim: On margin you can lose more than you put in.

facts.quote: A margin account allows you to borrow money from a brokerage firm to buy securities. This is also the only type of account in which investors can engage in short selling.
facts.claim: A margin account lets you borrow to buy, and it is the only account that allows short selling.

facts.quote: You may also enter into a short sale through a margin account, which involves you borrowing stock from a firm in order to sell it, hoping that the price will decline.
facts.claim: A short sale borrows stock to sell it, and it goes through a margin account.

facts.quote: In general, under Federal Reserve Board Regulation T, firms can lend a customer up to 50 percent of the total purchase price of a stock for new, or initial, purchases.
facts.claim: Under Regulation T, a broker can lend up to half the price of a new stock purchase.

facts.quote: Under these rules, as a general matter, your equity in the account must not fall below 25 percent of the current market value of the securities in the account.
facts.claim: FINRA's maintenance floor: your equity must stay at or above 25% of the stocks' current value.

facts.quote: your account equity would fall to $10,000 ($60,000 market value minus $50,000 loan amount).
facts.claim: Equity is the market value minus the margin loan.

facts.quote: Since the required equity is $15,000, your firm will likely issue a maintenance margin call for $5,000 ($15,000 less existing equity of $10,000).
facts.claim: The margin call is the required equity minus the equity you have.

facts.quote: Brokerage firms have the right to set their own maintenance margin requirements—often called "house" requirements—as long as they’re more stringent than the margin requirements under FINRA rules.
facts.claim: Brokers can set maintenance requirements stricter than FINRA's.

facts.quote: These changes in firm policy often take effect immediately and may result in the issuance of a maintenance margin call.
facts.claim: A broker's higher requirement can take effect at once and trigger a margin call.

facts.quote: You can lose more funds than you deposit in the margin account.
facts.claim: On margin you can lose more than you deposit.

facts.quote: The firm can sell your securities without notice.
facts.claim: The broker can sell your securities without telling you.

facts.quote: As a matter of customer relations, most firms will attempt to notify their customers of margin calls, but they aren’t required to do so.
facts.claim: Most brokers try to tell you about a margin call, but they don't have to.

facts.quote: You’re not entitled to an extension of time on a margin call.
facts.claim: You have no right to extra time on a margin call.

facts.quote: A firm charges interest for the money it lends its customers to purchase securities on margin
facts.claim: Margin interest is charged on the money the broker lends you.

facts.quote: With a cash account, you’re expected to pay the full amount for all securities purchased by the settlement date—which, for most securities, including options, means paying for them one day after you place an order to buy.
facts.claim: In a cash account, payment is due by settlement, one day after the buy, options included.

facts.quote: To estimate the potential loss in market value before incurring a maintenance call, use this formula: Current Maintenance Margin Excess ÷ (1.00 - maintenance requirement percentage)
facts.claim: FINRA's formula for how much value you can lose before a maintenance call: the margin excess divided by one minus the maintenance percent.

facts.quote: Some securities cannot be purchased on margin, which means they must be paid for in full
facts.claim: Some securities can't be bought on margin at all.

facts.quote: 25 percent of the current market value of all margin securities
facts.claim: Rule 4210's maintenance margin for long margin stocks is 25% of their current market value.

facts.quote: computed by adding the current market value of all securities "long" and the amount of any credit balance and subtracting the current market value of all securities "short" and the amount of any debit balance
facts.claim: Equity is what you own minus what you owe, including the margin loan (the debit balance).

facts.quote: Under the T+1 settlement cycle, most securities transactions settle on the next business day following their transaction date.
facts.claim: Under T+1, most trades settle the next business day.

facts.quote: For example, if you sell shares of a stock on Tuesday, the transaction will settle on Wednesday.
facts.claim: Sell on Tuesday and the sale settles Wednesday.

facts.quote: The T+1 settlement cycle applies to transactions for stocks, bonds, options, municipal securities, exchange-traded funds, certain mutual funds and U.S. government securities, and limited partnerships that trade on an exchange.
facts.claim: T+1 covers stocks, options, ETFs and bonds alike.

facts.quote: As of May 2024, the standard for settlement is next business day after a trade, or T+1.
facts.claim: Since May 2024, the standard settlement is T+1.

facts.quote: Since 2017, the settlement cycle – the time between the transaction date and the settlement date – for most securities transactions has been two business days – often referred to as “T+2.”
facts.claim: Before T+1, most trades settled in two business days (T+2).

facts.quote: The new “T+1” settlement cycle will apply to all applicable securities transactions occurring on or after May 28, 2024.
facts.claim: T+1 started with trades on or after May 28, 2024.

facts.quote: FINRA rules define a “pattern day trader” as any customer who executes four or more “day trades” within five business days
facts.claim: Under the old rule, four or more day trades in five business days made you a pattern day trader.

facts.quote: provided that the number of day trades represents more than six percent of the customer’s total trades in the margin account for that same five business day period.
facts.claim: The old count also required day trades to be more than 6% of your trades in the margin account in those five days.

facts.quote: Under FINRA rules, customers designated “pattern day traders” by their brokerage firms must have at least $25,000 in their accounts and can only trade in margin accounts.
facts.claim: Under the old rule, a pattern day trader needed at least $25,000, in a margin account.

facts.quote: The new intraday margin requirements, effective June 4, 2026, permit a transition period until October 20, 2027, for brokerage firms that need more time to comply.
facts.claim: The SEC's investor site confirms the change took effect June 4, 2026, with a transition to October 20, 2027.

facts.quote: If an investor buys and sells a security before paying for it, the investor is “freeriding”
facts.claim: Buying and selling before you pay is freeriding.

facts.quote: which is not permitted under the Federal Reserve Board’s Regulation T and may require the investor’s broker to “freeze” the investor’s cash account for 90 days.
facts.claim: Freeriding breaks Regulation T and can get the cash account frozen for 90 days.

facts.quote: During this 90-day period, an investor may still purchase securities with the cash account, but the investor must fully pay for any purchase on the date of the trade.
facts.claim: During a freeze you can still buy, but you pay in full on the trade date.

facts.quote: your brokerage firm can require you to deposit cash or securities to your account immediately, or sell any of the securities in your account to cover any shortfall, without informing you in advance.
facts.claim: On a margin call, the broker can demand money at once or sell your holdings without warning.

facts.quote: Even if the brokerage firm notifies you that you have a certain number of days to cover the shortfall, it still may sell your securities before then.
facts.claim: Even after giving you days to pay, the broker can sell sooner.

facts.quote: Margin increases investors’ purchasing power, but also exposes investors to the potential for larger losses.
facts.claim: Margin raises buying power and the size of possible losses.

facts.quote: 50 percent of the current market value of the security or the percentage set by the regulatory authority where the trade occurs, whichever is greater.
facts.claim: Regulation T's margin on a margin stock is 50% of its current value.

facts.quote: A good faith violation occurs when you buy a security and sell it before paying for the initial purchase in full with settled funds. Only cash or the sales proceeds of fully paid for securities qualify as "settled funds."
facts.claim: Selling a stock before it was paid for with settled funds is a good faith violation.

facts.quote: If Marty sells ABC stock prior to Tuesday (the settlement date of the XYZ sale), the transaction would be deemed a good faith violation
facts.claim: Fidelity's example: buy with Monday's sale proceeds and sell before they settle Tuesday, and it's a violation.

facts.quote: This trade is a violation because Trudy sold ABC before Monday's sale of XYZ stock settled and those proceeds became available to pay for the purchase of ABC stock
facts.claim: Starting the day with settled cash doesn't help: reusing a same-day sale and selling again that day is a violation.

facts.quote: If you incur three good faith violations in a 12-month period in a cash account, your brokerage firm will restrict your account.
facts.claim: At Fidelity, three good faith violations in 12 months restricts the cash account.

facts.quote: This means you will only be able to buy securities if you have sufficient settled cash in the account prior to placing a trade. This restriction will be effective for 90 calendar days.
facts.claim: The restriction means settled cash before every buy, for 90 days.

facts.quote: A freeriding violation occurs because Marty did not pay for the stock in full prior to selling it.
facts.claim: Selling a stock you never paid for is freeriding.

facts.quote: Making new buys in a correction is riskier, since most stocks will follow the market's downward trend.
facts.claim: New buys in a correction are riskier because most stocks follow the market down.

facts.quote: Use this time to look for stocks to add to your watch list so you'll be ready to take action when the market starts a new uptrend.
facts.claim: In a correction, build your watch list for the next uptrend.

facts.quote: Your goal is to make money when the market is trending higher and to protect your profits when it starts heading lower.
facts.claim: Make money in uptrends and protect it when the market turns down.

facts.quote: if the overall market is in a downtrend, it will be very hard for even the best stocks to move higher.
facts.claim: In a market downtrend, even the best stocks struggle to rise.

facts.quote: The biggest risk of market timing is usually considered not being in the market at critical times. Investors who try to time the market run the risk of missing periods of exceptional returns.
facts.claim: Being out of the market can mean missing its best stretches.

facts.quote: if an investor moves their money out of stocks during a market downturn, they risk not moving their money back in time to take advantage of gains from an upswing.
facts.claim: Go to cash in a downturn and you risk missing the upswing.

facts.quote: And they often end as abruptly as they began, with a quick rebound that is very difficult to predict
facts.claim: Bear markets often end with a quick rebound that is hard to predict.

facts.quote: Investors use a "cash is king" strategy when securities prices in the market are high and opt to save cash for when prices become cheaper.
facts.claim: Holding cash can be a deliberate choice, saved for better prices.

facts.quote: As a form of investment, it is important to not let cash sit idle but rather to invest so that returns are at least equal to inflation.
facts.claim: Idle cash loses ground to inflation over time.

facts.quote: CANSLIM stocks can quickly decline if the market shifts and institutional investors move to safer assets.
facts.claim: Growth leaders can fall fast when the market turns.

facts.quote: CANSLIM stocks tend to be over-performers in bull markets.
facts.claim: Growth stocks do their best work in bull markets.

facts.quote: However, investors must still weigh the risks involved with purchases, as they could well see a further decline as the correction continues.
facts.claim: Buying in a correction risks a further decline as it continues.

facts.quote: a dramatic correction that occurs in the course of one trading session can be disastrous for a short-term or day trader and those traders who are extremely leveraged.
facts.claim: A sharp correction can be disastrous for short-term traders on heavy margin.

facts.quote: A “margin account” is a type of brokerage account in which the broker-dealer lends the investor cash, using the account as collateral, to purchase securities.
facts.claim: In a margin account, the broker lends you cash to buy, with your account as collateral.

facts.quote: An investor using a cash account is not allowed to borrow funds from his or her broker-dealer in order to pay for transactions in the account
facts.claim: A cash account can't borrow from the broker.

walkthroughs.title: Margin is a loan
steps: A margin account lets you borrow from your broker. Under Regulation T, it can lend up to half of a new buy.
After that, FINRA's floor applies: your equity must not fall below 25% of the stock's value. Your broker can set it higher.
Drop under it and expect a margin call. The broker can sell your stock without telling you first.
Borrowed money grows your losses too. You can lose more than you put in.

walkthroughs.title: The day trading rule changed
steps: Old rule: four or more day trades in five business days made you a pattern day trader. Then you needed $25,000.
FINRA replaced it, effective June 4, 2026. No trade count, no $25,000. Your equity must cover your positions all day.
Brokers have until October 20, 2027 to switch. Until then, ask yours which rules your account runs on.

walkthroughs.title: Settled cash in a cash account
steps: Most trades settle T+1, the next business day. Sell on Tuesday and the cash settles on Wednesday.
Buy with cash that hasn't settled, then sell before it does, and that's a good faith violation.
Buy and sell before you pay at all, and that's freeriding. Your broker can freeze the account for 90 days.

questions.q: What does a margin account let you do?
choices: Borrow from your broker to buy
Cap your loss at what you deposit
Buy any stock with no money down
questions.answer: Borrow from your broker to buy
questions.why: Borrow from your broker to buy. The broker lends you cash, and your account backs the loan. That loan works both ways.
questions.lesson_line: Margin is a loan. It grows your buying power and your losses.

wrong.Cap your loss at what you deposit: Backwards. FINRA warns you can lose more than you deposit in a margin account.
wrong.Buy any stock with no money down: Regulation T has you put up part of a new buy yourself. Some securities can't be bought on margin at all.

questions.q: Your broker can sell your stock to meet a margin call without contacting you first.
questions.why: True. FINRA says your broker can sell your securities without notice. Most brokers try to reach you, but they don't have to.
questions.lesson_line: A margin call is not a conversation. Watch your equity before the broker has to.

questions.q: Tap the number that completes FINRA's rule.
questions.sentence: Your equity in a margin account must not fall below ___ of the stocks' current value.
questions.why: 25%. That's FINRA's maintenance floor for stocks you hold on margin. Your broker can set a higher house level.
questions.lesson_line: Know your broker's maintenance number. FINRA's is only the floor.

questions.q: Under Regulation T, how much of a new stock purchase can your broker lend you?
questions.why: Up to 50%. Regulation T lets brokers lend up to half the price of a new stock buy. You put up the rest.
questions.lesson_line: On a new buy, at least half is your own money.

wrong.Up to 25%: 25% is FINRA's maintenance floor, the equity you must keep later. It isn't the loan on a new buy.
wrong.Up to 75%: Too much. Regulation T caps the loan on a new stock buy at half the price.
wrong.Up to 100%: That's buying with none of your own money. Regulation T has you put up at least half.

questions.q: As of November 2026, FINRA's margin rule still sets a $25,000 minimum for pattern day traders.
questions.why: False. FINRA replaced the pattern day trader rules, the $25,000 minimum included, effective June 4, 2026. Brokers may phase in the change until October 20, 2027.
questions.lesson_line: The $25,000 rule is gone from FINRA's rulebook. Ask your broker whether it has switched yet.

questions.q: You sell shares on a Thursday, with no holiday that week. When does the sale settle?
questions.why: Friday. Most trades settle T+1, the next business day. FINRA's own example: sell on Tuesday, it settles on Wednesday.
questions.lesson_line: Trade date plus one business day. That's when the cash or the shares are really yours.

wrong.Thursday, the same day: That's the trade date. Settlement comes one business day later.
wrong.The next Monday: That's two business days, the old T+2 cycle. T+1 took over on May 28, 2024.

questions.q: Which kind of account do you need to sell a stock short?
questions.why: A margin account. A short sale borrows the stock to sell it, and FINRA says margin is the only account that allows it.
questions.lesson_line: No margin account, no short selling.

wrong.A cash account: A cash account can't borrow from the broker, and a short sale sells borrowed stock.
wrong.Either one works: Only a margin account allows short selling, because the stock you sell is borrowed.

questions.q: Options trades settle T+1, the same as stocks.
questions.why: True. FINRA lists options with stocks, bonds and ETFs under the T+1 cycle. In a cash account, you pay one day after you buy.
questions.lesson_line: Stock or option, the money is due one business day after the trade.

questions.q: You bought $20,000 of stock with a $10,000 margin loan. It's now worth $12,500. What's your equity as a percent of its value?
questions.why: 20%. Take the $10,000 loan off the $12,500 value, then divide by $12,500. That's under FINRA's 25% floor, so expect a margin call.
questions.lesson_line: Equity is value minus loan. On margin, check it as a percent every day.

questions.q: Cash account: you buy A with all your settled cash, sell it, then buy B with the proceeds. Selling B today is not a violation.
questions.why: False. Selling A was fine, because you paid for A with settled cash. B was paid with A's sale cash, which hasn't settled. Sell B today and that's a good faith violation.
questions.lesson_line: Settled cash can fund a same-day round trip. Cash from today's sale can't, until it settles.

questions.q: Under FINRA's rule as of November 2026, what's the least equity you need to borrow on margin?
questions.why: $2,000. That's FINRA's minimum equity to trade on margin. Your broker can ask for more as a house rule.
questions.lesson_line: FINRA's floor to borrow is $2,000. Your broker's minimum may be higher.

wrong.$25,000: That was the old minimum for pattern day traders, not the floor to borrow. FINRA's new rule dropped it.
wrong.No minimum at all: Under $2,000 you can still trade in a margin account, but only with your own cash, no borrowing.

questions.q: $40,000 of stock bought with a $20,000 margin loan falls to $24,000. Using FINRA's 25% floor, how big is the margin call?
questions.why: $2,000. You need 25% of $24,000 in equity. You have $24,000 less the $20,000 loan. The call is the gap.
questions.lesson_line: The call is the equity you need minus the equity you have.

questions.q: You put up $10,000 and borrow $10,000 to buy $20,000 of stock. It falls 30%. Ignoring interest, what percent of your money is lost?
questions.why: 60%. A 30% drop on $20,000 of stock comes out of your $10,000 alone. Borrowing doubled your loss.
questions.lesson_line: Borrow half the position and every drop hits your money twice as hard.

questions.story: Cash account with no settled cash. Monday morning you sell XYZ. Monday afternoon you buy ABC with that money.
questions.q: When can you sell ABC without a good faith violation?
choices: Only after you add new cash
questions.why: Once XYZ's sale has settled. Sell ABC before then and you've sold a stock bought with unsettled money. In Fidelity's example, selling before XYZ settles on Tuesday is a violation.
questions.lesson_line: Bought with unsettled cash means you hold it until that cash settles.

wrong.Right away, XYZ already sold: Sold isn't settled. XYZ's cash settles the next business day, not when the sale fills.
wrong.Only after you add new cash: No new money needed. XYZ's proceeds pay for ABC once they settle.

questions.story: Cash account with $0 in it. Monday you buy $5,000 of a stock and send no money. Wednesday you sell it for $5,400 to cover the cost.
questions.q: What did you just do?
choices: A good faith violation on the sale
Nothing wrong, it made a profit
questions.why: Freeriding. You bought and sold before paying for it. Regulation T doesn't allow that, and your broker can freeze the cash account for 90 days.
questions.lesson_line: Pay for it before you sell it. A freeze means paying in full on the trade date for 90 days.

wrong.A good faith violation on the sale: Close, but that's selling a stock bought with unsettled sale cash. You never paid at all, and that's freeriding.
wrong.Nothing wrong, it made a profit: Profit doesn't fix it. You sold the stock before you paid for it.

questions.story: Your broker has switched to FINRA's new intraday margin rule. You day trade a few times a week in a $15,000 margin account.
questions.q: What does the new rule check?
choices: Day trades counted over five days
questions.why: Your equity against your positions, all through the day. No trade count, no $25,000 minimum. Come up short and you have an intraday margin deficit to cover promptly.
questions.lesson_line: The new rule doesn't count your trades. It checks your equity, all day.

wrong.Day trades counted over five days: That was the old pattern day trader count. The new rule has no trade count.
wrong.A $25,000 minimum balance to trade: The new rule has no $25,000 minimum for day trading.
wrong.Nothing, day trading is unlimited: Run short of equity and you owe an intraday margin deficit. Keep missing them and the account can be restricted for up to 90 days.

questions.story: $20,000 margin account. You make four day trades in five business days, and no other trades. Your broker still runs the old day trading rules.
questions.q: What happens?
choices: Nothing until a fifth day trade
questions.why: You're flagged as a pattern day trader. Under the old rule, four day trades in five business days does it, and you need $25,000 to keep going. Brokers may run the old rules until October 20, 2027.
questions.lesson_line: Know which rules your broker runs. The old count still bites until it switches.

wrong.Nothing, FINRA dropped that rule: FINRA did, but brokers can phase the change in. Until yours switches, the old count and the $25,000 minimum apply.
wrong.Nothing until a fifth day trade: The old rule kicks in at four or more day trades in five business days, not five.

questions.story: Cash account. Twice this month you bought with cash from a same-day sale. Both times the new stock hit its stop and you sold it that day.
questions.q: What's the best habit to stop this happening again?
choices: Hold losers until the cash settles
Sell with a limit order instead
questions.why: Buy only with settled cash. Then you can sell the moment your stop hits. Those were two good faith violations, and at Fidelity three in 12 months restricts the account for 90 days.
questions.lesson_line: Trade a cash account with settled cash, so your stop is always free to work.

wrong.Hold losers until the cash settles: That swaps a rule problem for risk you never planned. Your stop was the plan.
wrong.Sell with a limit order instead: The order type doesn't matter. Selling before the cash settles is the violation.

questions.q: Under FINRA's new intraday rule, the 25% maintenance floor applies all day, not just at the close.
questions.why: True. You must hold 25% maintenance margin throughout the entire trading day, not just at the end. Your broker can set a higher number.
questions.lesson_line: On margin, a bad hour counts, not just a bad close.

questions.story: You hold a volatile stock on margin. Your equity is 35% of its value. Your broker raises its house requirement on that stock to 40%, starting today.
questions.q: What should you expect?
choices: A week's notice before any sale
questions.why: A margin call, right away. Brokers can set house requirements above FINRA's 25%, and those changes often take effect immediately. You aren't owed extra time.
questions.lesson_line: FINRA's 25% is the floor. Your broker's number is the one that calls you.

wrong.Nothing, FINRA's floor is 25%: Your broker can require more than FINRA's floor, and its number is the one you have to meet.
wrong.Nothing until your next buy: House changes often take effect immediately and can trigger a call on what you already hold.
wrong.A week's notice before any sale: You're not entitled to extra time, and the broker can sell without notice.

questions.q: You buy $20,000 of stock with a $9,000 margin loan. How far, in percent, can it fall before your equity hits FINRA's 25% floor?
questions.why: 40%. The $9,000 loan stays the same while the stock falls. After a 40% drop, your equity is down to 25% of what's left. Any lower and expect a call.
questions.lesson_line: Know the drop that triggers a margin call before you borrow, not after.

questions.q: Going to cash protects you when stocks fall. What does it cost you?
choices: You can miss a sharp rebound
questions.answer: You can miss a sharp rebound
questions.why: You can miss a sharp rebound. Bear markets often end abruptly, with a quick rebound that's hard to predict. Out at the wrong time, you miss the upswing.
questions.lesson_line: Going to cash is a trade too. It has a payoff and a cost.

wrong.Margin interest on the cash: Interest is charged on money you borrow. Cash you hold isn't a loan.
wrong.Nothing at all: Idle cash can lose ground to inflation, and you can miss the upswing.

questions.story: The market is in a correction. Your last five breakouts failed within days. Few stocks are holding their moves.
questions.q: What's the best use of your account now?
choices: More cash, and build a watch list
Keep buying breakouts at full size
Borrow on margin to buy the dip
Size up to win the losses back
questions.answer: More cash, and build a watch list
questions.why: More cash, and build the list. New buys in a correction are riskier, since most stocks follow the market down. Use the time to find stocks for the next uptrend.
questions.lesson_line: Cash is a position. In a correction, I'd rather hold cash and a sharp watch list.

wrong.Keep buying breakouts at full size: Your results say the market is against breakouts right now. New buys in a correction are riskier.
wrong.Borrow on margin to buy the dip: A correction can keep going. Borrowing into it grows your losses, and you can lose more than you put in.
wrong.Size up to win the losses back: Bigger size where most breakouts fail means bigger losses. New buys in a correction are riskier, not safer.

conflicts: The pattern day trader rule changed this year. FINRA Regulatory Notice 26-10 (April 20, 2026) replaced the day trading margin requirements in their entirety, the four-in-five-days count and the $25,000 minimum included, effective June 4, 2026, with a phase-in for brokers until October 20, 2027. The current Rule 4210 text (version Oct 22, 2026 onwards, read 2026-11-09) has no pattern day trader provisions. Investor.gov's 'Pattern Day Trader' glossary still prints the old definition under a banner announcing the change. The plan row's practise case ('four day trades on a 20k account') assumed the old rule; the file teaches the old rule only as what a broker that has not switched may still run (w2, q17), keys the current rule as 'FINRA's rule as of November 2026' (q05, q11, q16, q19), and sets as_of 2026-11-09.

FINRA's Brokerage Accounts page, margin tip: '$25,000 ÷ (1.00 – 0.25) = $33,337'. The arithmetic gives $33,333.33. The file quotes FINRA's formula (f35) but never the $33,337 figure; q21 computes its own number through a calc.

Going to cash: IBD (CAN SLIM's M) says new buys in a correction are riskier and to protect profits when the market heads lower; Investopedia's CANSLIM and Correction pages agree that growth stocks fall when the market shifts and that buying in a correction risks a further decline. Investopedia's Market Timing and Schwab's correction pages say long-term investors usually do better staying invested, because rebounds are abrupt and hard to predict. The file asks the cash question for an active swing trader whose breakouts are failing (q23) and teaches the cost of cash from Investopedia and Schwab (q22), so both halves are shown. q23 drops a 'stay fully invested' choice, because for a long-term investor it is a defensible answer.

Good faith violation consequences ('three good faith violations in a 12-month period' then a 90-day settled-cash restriction) are Fidelity's stated practice, not a FINRA or SEC rule. FINRA defines the violation (f15) and the file keys only that; the count is named as Fidelity's in q18's why.

Selling on the settlement date itself: Fidelity's example calls it a violation to sell 'prior to Tuesday (the settlement date of the XYZ sale)', which implies a sale on Tuesday is fine, but no Tier 1 page says so outright. q14 keys 'once XYZ's sale has settled' and never asks about the settlement day itself.

Margin call size: FINRA's example sizes the call to bring equity back to the 25% minimum; brokers can ask for more (house requirements). q12 says 'using FINRA's 25% floor' so the number is FINRA's method, not any one broker's.

Checker 2026-11-09, how the new rule is watched: FINRA's Investor Insights say 'your firm monitors your account ... during the trading day', but Regulatory Notice 26-10 says real-time monitoring 'is not a requirement' and firms may make 'a single calculation' of the intraday deficit, and the same Insight says a firm may compute it 'at the end of the trading day'. The file therefore teaches that the requirement applies all day (f06, f12) and no longer says the broker checks all day (w2 changed).

w1.notes: f75 (Investor.gov Margin Account), f23, f24, f27, f30, f29 (FINRA Brokerage Accounts) and f52 (Investor.gov Margin Call) read in context on the live pages 2026-11-09; the 50% loan, the 25% floor and house levels match. Changed step 3 'you get a margin call' to 'expect a margin call': FINRA says you 'may be required' to deposit and the firm 'will likely' issue a call.

w2.notes: f45/f47 (Investor.gov glossary, old rule printed under a 2026 change banner), f01/f02 (Notice 26-10) and f06/f12/f09 (FINRA Insight) read live. Current Rule 4210 (version Oct 22, 2026 onwards) has no pattern day trader text; Notice 26-21 (Oct 2026) is about binary options and a search found no change to the phase-in, so June 4, 2026 and October 20, 2027 stand. Changed: 'four day trades' to 'four or more'; 'Your broker checks your margin all day' to 'Your equity must cover your positions all day', because Notice 26-10 lets brokers make a single end-of-day calculation (see conflicts); f12 added.

w3.notes: f39/f40 (FINRA Understanding Settlement Cycles, May 7, 2026: the first plain fetch got a 429, a second fetch and WebFetch both showed the text), f15 (FINRA Frequent Intraday Trading, June 4, 2026) and f49/f50 (Investor.gov Freeriding) read in context. Tuesday sale settling Wednesday is FINRA's own example; the 90-day freeze is the SEC page's 'may require ... freeze'.

q01.notes: Key from f75 (Investor.gov: the broker lends cash, the account is collateral) and f21 (FINRA). Wrong choices are real beliefs: f29 'You can lose more funds than you deposit' breaks the cap; f23 and f36 break 'no money down'. Answer is 30 characters, fits a Word Match tile. Split the 25-word wrong note into two sentences.

q02.notes: f30 and f31 (FINRA: the firm can sell 'without notice'; most firms try to notify 'but they aren't required to') and f52 (Investor.gov: 'without informing you in advance') read in context. True as stated.

q03.notes: f24 (FINRA, 'as a general matter' 25% of current market value) and f37 (Rule 4210(c)(1), current version) confirmed. Bank distractors are numbers members mix up (50% is Reg T's initial margin). The why names house levels (f27).

q04.notes: f23 (FINRA: 'up to 50 percent of the total purchase price ... for new, or initial, purchases') and f55 (eCFR 12 CFR 220.12(a), current: 50 percent) confirmed. Wrong notes right: 25% is the maintenance floor (f24); 75% and 100% exceed Regulation T.

q05.notes: Key False: Notice 26-10 replaced the day trading requirements 'in their entirety', the $25,000 minimum included, effective June 4, 2026 (f01, f02); the current Rule 4210 text has no pattern day trader provision; f05 and f09 from the FINRA Insight. The why gives the phase-in to October 20, 2027, so a member at a broker that has not switched is not misled.

q06.notes: T+1 per f39/f42 (FINRA) and f44 (SEC bulletin, March 27, 2024: trades on or after May 28, 2024). Thursday plus one business day is Friday, and the question rules out a holiday. 'The next Monday' is Thursday plus two business days, the old T+2 (f43). Choice lengths differ but none gives the key away.

q07.notes: f21 (FINRA: margin is 'the only type of account in which investors can engage in short selling'), f22 and f76 (Investor.gov: a cash account can't borrow) confirmed. Wrong notes right.

q08.notes: f41 (FINRA settlement page lists options under T+1) and f34 (FINRA Brokerage Accounts: 'for most securities, including options, ... one day after') confirmed. The SEC's 2024 bulletin lists no options, but options already settled next day, so nothing conflicts with the statement.

q09.notes: Recomputed (12,500 - 10,000) / 12,500 = 20%; calc margin_equity_pct matches. Equity is value minus loan per f38 (Rule 4210(a)(5)) and FINRA's worked example f25. 20% is under the 25% floor (f24), and FINRA says the firm 'will likely issue' a call, so 'expect a margin call' is fair.

q10.notes: Rebuilt. The old statement ('you can buy and sell a second stock today ...') was ambiguous, since the broker takes the order, and it tested the same case as q14. It is now Fidelity's Trudy case (f58): settled cash pays for A, A's unsettled proceeds buy B, and selling B the same day is a good faith violation. Key False rests on FINRA f15 (Tier 1: selling before 'the proceeds used to fund the purchase have settled') with Fidelity f56/f58. Lesson line written so it does not imply one round trip a day.

q11.notes: $2,000 from FINRA f10 and f18 (current) and Rule 4210(b)(4), 'equity of at least $2,000', read on the current rule page. 'No minimum at all' is wrong per f11. Changed the '$25,000' note: 'some brokers may still run the old rules' hinted that $25,000 might be the floor to borrow at those brokers; it now says $25,000 was the pattern day trader minimum, never the floor to borrow.

q12.notes: Recomputed: required 25% x $24,000 = $6,000; equity $24,000 - $20,000 = $4,000; call $2,000. Calc matches. Method is FINRA's own example (f26: $15,000 less $10,000 = a $5,000 call), read in context.

q13.notes: Recomputed 30% x $20,000 = $6,000 lost; $6,000 / $10,000 = 60%; calc matches. At $14,000 equity is 28.6%, still above 25%, so no forced sale muddies the number. f54 (SEC: larger losses), f29 and f20 (FINRA) carry the lesson.

q14.notes: Fidelity's Marty example (f57) read in context: $0 settled cash, sell XYZ Monday morning, buy ABC Monday afternoon, selling ABC 'prior to Tuesday' is a violation. FINRA f15 (Tier 1) defines it the same way, so the key holds. 'Only after you add new cash' is wrong because of 'only': waiting for settlement is enough. The settlement-day edge case is not asked (see conflicts).

q15.notes: Mirrors Fidelity's freeriding example (f61: $0 cash, buy Monday, no payment by Tuesday, sell Wednesday to cover). SEC f49/f50 (Tier 1): buying and selling before paying is freeriding, not permitted under Regulation T, and can bring a 90-day freeze; f51 for the freeze's terms. A good faith violation is the near miss (FINRA f15 ties it to unsettled sale cash), and the wrong note says why. | variety rewrite checked 2026-11-10

q16.notes: f06, f05, f07, f08 from the FINRA Insight (April 20, 2026) read in context: no trade count, no $25,000, equity relative to positions during the trading day, a deficit to satisfy 'as promptly as possible', up to 90 days restricted for repeat failures. The story says the broker has switched, so the key holds without conditions. | variety rewrite checked 2026-11-10

q17.notes: Old rule per f45/f46/f47 (Investor.gov glossary, still printed under the 2026 banner): four or more day trades in five business days, more than 6% of trades ('no other trades' makes it 100%), $25,000 minimum. f09 and f02: brokers may run the old rules until October 20, 2027, which the story states. This is the plan's practise case (four day trades on a $20,000 account). | variety rewrite checked 2026-11-10

q18.notes: Key from FINRA f17 (Tier 1): to trade intraday in a cash account, pay at purchase with settled funds. f15 makes both trades good faith violations; Fidelity f59/f60 (named as Fidelity's practice) for three in 12 months and 90 days. Changed 'What habit keeps this from happening again?' to 'What's the best habit ...': holding losers until the cash settles also avoids the violation, so the question has to ask for the best habit, and the wrong note explains the cost (a stop you skipped).

q19.notes: f12 confirmed verbatim: 25% maintenance 'throughout the entire trading day, not just at end of the day'; f13 for house levels; f04 (Notice 26-10: the new rule supplements maintenance margin). A different angle from q16 (when the 25% applies, not what replaced the trade count).

q20.notes: f27 and f28 (FINRA: house requirements can apply to particular volatile stocks and 'often take effect immediately and may result in the issuance of a maintenance margin call'), f32 (no right to an extension) and f30 (sale without notice) read in context. Equity of 35% under a 40% house level that starts today: a call is what to expect.

q21.notes: Recomputed: the floor is hit when V - 9,000 = 0.25V, so V = $12,000, a 40% drop from $20,000; at $12,000 equity is $3,000 = 25%. FINRA's formula (f35) agrees: excess $11,000 - $5,000 = $6,000, / 0.75 = $8,000 = 40%. $11,000 down is above Regulation T's 50%. Calc matches.

q22.notes: Investopedia f66/f67 (missing the upswing is the biggest risk of being out) and Schwab f68 (bear markets 'often end as abruptly as they began, with a quick rebound that is very difficult to predict') agree: two Tier 2 publishers. In the Schwab text 'they' is bear markets, as the why says. Wrong notes: f33 (interest is on money lent) and f70 (cash should earn at least inflation). | variety rewrite checked 2026-11-10

q23.notes: IBD f62/f63/f64 (new buys in a correction are riskier; build the watch list; protect profits) and Investopedia f71/f73/f74 (growth stocks fall fast when the market shifts; buying in a correction risks a further decline; heavy leverage is disastrous in a sharp correction) agree. Wrong choices are named mistakes, with f29 for the margin note. Trading sense: raising cash and building the list is standard growth-trader discipline; the long-term-investor view is in conflicts and not offered as a choice.
